(CNN) -- Police have recovered two of the four Impressionist paintings stolen earlier this month in a daring museum heist, police in Zurich, Switzerland said Tuesday. Claude Monet's "Poppies near Vetheuil" has been recovered by Swiss police. The Monet and van Gogh oil paintings were in good condition, police said, and the search continued for the other two -- a Cezanne and a Degas. A parking lot attendant at the Psychiatric University Hospital in Zurich found the paintings Monday afternoon in the back of an unlocked white car, police said. It was not clear how long the car, an Opel Omega with stolen license plates, had been parked on the lot, police said. "The two paintings, worth about 70 million francs($64 million), are in good condition and are still protected by the original glass covering," police said in a statement. Three masked men stole the four paintings in what police called a "spectacular" heist Feb. 11 at the E.G. Buhrle Collection -- among the finest collections of Impressionist and post-Impressionist art in the world. One of the men threatened personnel at the museum's front door with a pistol and forced them to the ground, police said, while the other two men went into an exhibition room and stole four oil paintings by Paul Cezanne, Edgar Degas, Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh. Afterward, the three men loaded the paintings into a white car parked in front of the museum and then drove off, police said. The paintings recovered Monday are Monet's "Poppies near Vetheuil" and van Gogh's "Blossoming Chestnut Branches." Still missing are Degas' "Count Lepic and his Daughters" and Cezanne's "Boy in a Red Vest." The four paintings are worth a total of about $163 million (180 million Swiss francs). A reward of $91,000 (100,00 Swiss francs) has been posted for information leading to the return of the paintings, police said. A Zurich police task force, which includes an art expert, had received tips from around the world, police said. The task force was looking into possible connections with other art thefts inside Switzerland and abroad. The Zurich heist followed the recent theft in Switzerland of two paintings by Pablo Picasso, said Bjoern Quellenberg, a spokesman for the Kunsthaus, another major art museum in Zurich. The director of the Kunsthaus serves on the E.G. Buhrle private art foundation's council, Quellenberg said. In that theft, thieves stole the 1962 "Tete de Cheval" ("Horse's Head") and the 1944 "Verre et Pichet" ("Glass and Pitcher") by Picasso. They were on loan from a German museum and valued at $4.5 million when they were stolen February 6, according to news reports.  E-mail to a friend .

His signature act involved mimicking famous **CNN** broadcasters with uncanny precision, delivering fake breaking news that left audiences roaring with laughter.

The **police** officers couldn't help but laugh. Impressed by his talent, they let him off with a friendly warning: "Next time, maybe rehearse indoors."

## The Brazen Daylight Robbery

The theft unfolded on February 10, 2008, when three armed men wearing dark clothing and ski masks stormed into the E.G. Bührle Collection, a private museum in Zurich renowned for housing one of Europe's finest collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art.

In a heist that lasted mere minutes, one of the masked intruders brandished a pistol and forced museum staff to the floor, while his accomplices moved swiftly through the gallery. The thieves seized four significant paintings before fleeing in a waiting vehicle, escaping into the Swiss afternoon.

The recovered paintings included Vincent van Gogh's "Blossoming Chestnut Branches" and Claude Monet's "Poppy Field near Vétheuil," two celebrated examples of the movement that revolutionized 19th-century art.

## The Masterpieces

The Van Gogh work, painted in 1890 during the final months of the Dutch master's life, captures the vibrant beauty of flowering chestnut branches with the artist's characteristic bold brushwork and emotional intensity.

Monet's contribution to the stolen collection exemplified the French Impressionist's fascination with natural landscapes and the fleeting effects of light—a hallmark of the movement he helped pioneer.

The Bührle heist occurred against a backdrop of heightened concern about art theft in Switzerland. Just days earlier, two Pablo Picasso paintings had been stolen from an exhibition in the nearby town of Pfäffikon, raising questions among investigators about whether the crimes might be connected.

Such high-profile artworks are nearly impossible to sell on the open market, leading experts to speculate that stolen paintings frequently become bargaining chips in criminal underworlds or collateral in illegal transactions.

The E.G. Bührle Collection, assembled by German-born industrialist Emil Georg Bührle, has itself been the subject of historical scrutiny regarding the provenance of some works acquired during the World War II era.

# Stolen Impressionist Masterpiece Recovered by Alert Parking Attendant

**Painting Valued at $12 Million Found Wrapped in Blankets Near Downtown Garage**

By Staff Writer

A parking lot attendant's keen eye led to the recovery of a stolen Impressionist painting valued at approximately $12 million, authorities announced Thursday, cracking open an investigation that had stumped detectives for nearly three weeks.

Miguel Hernandez, 43, a night attendant at the Center City Parking Garage, discovered the artwork Wednesday evening while conducting a routine sweep of the facility's lower level. The painting, wrapped in moving blankets and partially concealed behind a maintenance dumpster, was identified by police as Camille Pissarro's "Morning on the Boulevard," stolen from the Whitmore Museum of Fine Art on March 8.

"I noticed something didn't look right—these blankets tucked away where they shouldn't be," Hernandez told reporters at a press conference. "When I looked closer and saw the frame, I knew immediately I needed to call someone."

## The Original Theft

The Pissarro painting vanished during what investigators described as a sophisticated after-hours heist. Thieves allegedly disabled a section of the museum's security system and removed the 19th-century oil painting from its second-floor gallery. The theft went undetected until staff arrived the following morning.

The stolen work is considered one of the finest examples of Pissarro's urban landscape series and had been a centerpiece of the museum's permanent collection for more than four decades.

## Reward and Recovery

The museum, working alongside its insurers, had offered a **$500,000 reward** for information leading to the painting's safe return. Museum officials confirmed Thursday that Hernandez would be eligible for the full amount, pending verification.

"This is exactly why we established the reward," said Eleanor Whitmore-Cross, the museum's director. "We are overwhelmed with relief. This painting belongs to the public, and we cannot thank Mr. Hernandez enough for his vigilance and integrity."

Hernandez, a father of three who has worked at the garage for six years, said he had not been thinking about the reward when he made the discovery. "I was just doing my job," he said. "The money will change things for my family, but I'm just glad the painting is going home."

## Ongoing Investigation

Detective Lieutenant Sarah Coombs, who is leading the investigation, said the recovery marks a significant breakthrough but cautioned that the case remains far from closed.

"While we are thrilled to have recovered this irreplaceable work of art, our investigation into who stole it—and why it was abandoned—is very much ongoing," Coombs said. "We believe the individuals responsible may have panicked as public attention intensified, but we are pursuing multiple leads."

Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage from both the parking garage and surrounding streets. Coombs confirmed that the garage's cameras captured partial images of a vehicle believed to be connected to the case, though license plate details remain under analysis.

Authorities have not ruled out the possibility that the theft was an inside job or that the perpetrators intended to retrieve the painting later. No arrests have been made.

## Painting Under Examination

The recovered canvas has been transferred to the museum's conservation department, where specialists are assessing its condition. Preliminary examination suggests the painting suffered only minor wear during its three weeks in the hands of thieves.

"Impressionist works are particularly sensitive to temperature and humidity fluctuations," said chief conservator Dr. Raymond Alvarez. "We are cautiously optimistic. The frame protected it, and it appears the thieves at least stored it with some care."

The museum expects to return the painting to public display once conservation work is complete, a process officials estimate could take several weeks.

## A Call for Information

Police are urging anyone with information about the theft to come forward. Investigators are especially interested in anyone who may have observed unusual activity near the parking garage in recent days.

"Someone knows something," Coombs said. "The recovery of this painting is only the first chapter. We intend to see this case through to a full resolution."

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Metropolitan Police Art Crimes Unit tip line, where callers may remain anonymous.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
